identification.title: Indescribable
identification.notes: Written by Laura Story with Jesse Reeves. Recorded by Chris Tomlin on Arriving (2004), which is how most congregations know it, though the song is Story's.

claims.structuralNotes: Two verses over a repeated chorus with a bridge. The verses catalogue creation — storms, seasons, stars — and the chorus draws the conclusion that God exceeds description.

claims.claim: God made the storms, the seasons and the depths of the earth.
claims.subject: Creation

claims.claim: God counts the stars and calls them each by name.
claims.subject: God's knowledge
claims.lyricExcerpt: You count the stars and You call them by name

claims.claim: God is indescribable, uncontainable and beyond understanding.
claims.subject: The incomprehensibility of God

claims.claim: Creation itself declares God's greatness back to him.
claims.subject: Creation's witness

claims.claim: God is amazing, and the singer worships him for it.
claims.subject: Worship

strengths.title: Argues from what God made to who God is
strengths.explanation: The verses do the work before the chorus draws the conclusion. A congregation is given evidence rather than an assertion, which is how Psalm 19 and Romans 1 proceed.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The heavens declare the glory of God — creation as testimony, which is the verses' method.

strengths.title: Names God's knowledge of particulars
strengths.explanation: Counting the stars and naming each one is a claim about God knowing individuals, not merely about his being large. It is the line in the song with the most weight and it is taken from the psalter.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: You count the stars and You call them by name
strengths.scriptureRationale: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.

strengths.title: Incomprehensibility stated as the conclusion, not the premise
strengths.explanation: The chorus says God exceeds description only after the verses have tried to describe him. The order matters: the confession is earned rather than asserted.
strengths.scriptureRationale: How unsearchable his judgements and how inscrutable his ways.

concerns.title: A God of creation with no mention of redemption
concerns.explanation: The song is entirely about God as maker. Christ, the cross and salvation appear nowhere, so a congregation is taught to marvel at the Creator without being told he is also the Redeemer.
concerns.scriptureRationale: The one through whom all things were created is the one who reconciles by the blood of his cross — Paul holds together what the song separates.

theological.assessment: A creation psalm in modern dress, and it follows the psalter's method: evidence first, conclusion second. The line about God naming the stars is a real claim about his knowledge of individuals rather than a general statement of size, and the chorus's confession of incomprehensibility is earned by the verses that precede it. What it never does is move from Creator to Redeemer — the God who made the storms is not identified as the one who died.

strengths.title: A chorus of four adjectives a room can hold
strengths.explanation: Short, strong words on a rising line. Congregations have kept this song for twenty years partly because the chorus is impossible to forget.

strengths.title: Structure with no traps
strengths.explanation: Two verses, a chorus, a bridge, no key change and no rhythmic hook that depends on the recording. It works with a small band.

concerns.title: The chorus climbs above the verses
concerns.explanation: The song's memorable line is also its highest, and it recurs. Rooms sing the verses comfortably and strain at the part they most want to sing.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in G and A. The chorus is the demanding part and returns often; pitch for it rather than for the verses.

range.key: Commonly published in G and A
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus repeats a short list of adjectives. What returns is a confession about God's nature rather than a hook, though the list is short enough that it wears with heavy use.
communal.assessment: Durable and straightforward, with a structure that holds no surprises for a congregation or a small band. The one practical difficulty is that the chorus — the part everyone wants to sing — sits above the rest of the song.

strengths.title: Concrete pictures, not abstractions
strengths.explanation: Storms, seasons and stars are things a hearer can see. The song builds its case out of the visible before making a claim about the invisible.

strengths.title: Verses and chorus in an obvious relationship
strengths.explanation: Evidence then conclusion, repeatedly. The logic is audible without being explained.

concerns.title: Which God, exactly, is left open
concerns.explanation: A God who made the world and exceeds description is a claim many religions would sign. Nothing in the song names Christ or narrows it to the Christian God, so the identification comes from the room rather than the text.

clarity.assessment: Vivid and logically clear — the verses show and the chorus concludes. Its openness is at the level of identity rather than meaning: everything said is true of God, and nothing said is true only of the God who became flesh.

synthesis.summary: A creation psalm in modern dress that follows the psalter's method — evidence first, conclusion second. Its claim about God naming the stars is a real statement about his knowledge of individuals, and the confession of incomprehensibility is earned by the verses that precede it. What it never does is move from Creator to Redeemer.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Creation as testimony, which is the verses' method.
God numbering and naming the stars — the song's weightiest line.
Unsearchable ways, the conclusion the chorus draws.
Creator and Redeemer held together, which the song separates.
